questions.q: Why is base62 commonly used to encode short URL keys?
options: It encrypts the underlying numeric ID so users cannot guess other links
It is the densest encoding that URLs can legally carry
It avoids collisions by construction, unlike hashing
It packs IDs into short strings using only URL-safe alphanumerics
questions.explanation: Base62 uses only 0-9, a-z, A-Z, which need no percent-encoding in a URL, and its wide alphabet keeps codes short. It is encoding, not encryption, so it hides nothing.

questions.q: Roughly how many distinct 7-character base62 codes exist?
options: About 62 times 7, on the order of hundreds
62^7, on the order of trillions
7^62, an astronomically larger number
2^7, exactly 128 possible codes
questions.explanation: Each of the 7 positions independently holds one of 62 symbols, giving 62^7, about 3.5 trillion codes, which is why 7 characters is the usual default length.

questions.q: What is the core read-path flow when a user hits a short link?
options: Recompute a hash of the short code to mathematically derive the original URL
Query the analytics store, then reconstruct the target from logs
Look up the code in a key-value store and issue an HTTP redirect
Proxy the target page's content through the shortener's servers
questions.explanation: The service is a lookup plus a 301/302 Location header; the browser then fetches the target itself. Codes are not reversible, so the mapping must be stored.

questions.q: Why is a URL shortener's workload described as read-heavy?
options: Each link is created once but may be clicked thousands of times
Redirect responses are larger than link-creation requests
Analytics writes are batched, leaving reads as the only online path
Browsers prefetch every short link before users click it
questions.explanation: One write creates a mapping that then serves an unbounded number of redirects, giving read-to-write ratios of 100:1 or more and making caching the dominant optimization.

questions.q: Which storage model fits the core mapping of a URL shortener?
options: A graph database relating codes to users to campaigns
A document store holding one JSON blob per customer
A key-value store mapping short code to long URL
A columnar warehouse partitioned by creation date
questions.explanation: The access pattern is a single point lookup by primary key with no joins or scans, which is exactly what a key-value store does at low latency and easy horizontal scale.

questions.q: A 301 redirect differs from a 302 mainly in that browsers will:
options: Cache the 301 and often skip contacting the shortener next time
Display an interstitial warning page before following any 301 redirect
Refuse to follow 301s across different domains
Retry a 301 with POST if the first request used GET
questions.explanation: 301 means permanently moved, so browsers cache the mapping and go straight to the target. That saves load but hides later clicks from your analytics and pins stale targets.

questions.q: Why does hashing the long URL (MD5, then truncating) require collision handling?
options: Hash outputs vary between servers, so codes are irreproducible
MD5 is slow enough to bottleneck the write path at scale
Truncation makes codes case-sensitive, which URLs forbid
Different URLs can truncate to the same short code
questions.explanation: Truncating to ~7 characters shrinks the output space enormously, so by pigeonhole plus the birthday bound distinct URLs will eventually map to the same prefix.

questions.q: What is the simplest collision-free key generation scheme?
options: Hash the URL and probe until an unused code is found
Encode a globally unique auto-incrementing ID in base62
Generate random codes without checking the database
Derive the code from the request's timestamp in milliseconds
questions.explanation: A monotonically increasing ID is unique by construction, and base62 encoding is a bijection, so no collision check or retry loop is ever needed.

questions.q: You want click analytics per link but chose 301 redirects. What's the standard resolution?
options: Parse browser cache logs shipped nightly by a client-side script
Use 302/307 so each click reaches the server, trading redirect caching away
Keep 301 but ask CDNs to forward their access logs weekly
Embed a tracking pixel into every destination page at the exact moment of redirect
questions.explanation: 302/307 are temporary, so browsers re-request each time and every click hits your servers to be counted. The cost is extra load that caching would have avoided.

questions.q: A single-range auto-increment counter becomes a write bottleneck and single point of failure. What's the common fix?
options: Locking the counter row in a serializable transaction per write
Switching to UUIDv4 codes truncated to seven characters
A ticket/segment service that leases ID ranges to app servers
Hashing timestamps with server IDs to avoid coordination
questions.explanation: Each server leases a block of IDs and hands them out locally, so coordination happens once per thousands of links instead of once per write, and uniqueness still holds.

questions.q: Redirect p99 latency must stay near 20ms globally. Which architecture serves that best?
options: Cache hot mappings at edge locations or CDN with the store as origin
One strongly consistent primary region with very fast SSDs
Client-side resolution using a downloaded mapping bundle
Synchronous multi-region writes so all replicas stay identical
questions.explanation: Speed of light makes cross-continent round trips alone exceed 20ms, so the answer must terminate the request near the user; a single region cannot beat physics.

questions.q: Users can pick custom aliases. Two requests race for 'summer-sale'. What prevents both from succeeding?
options: Optimistic retries that regenerate a random alias for the loser
Application-level check-then-insert performed inside a cache
Sharding aliases so racing requests land on different nodes
A unique constraint or atomic conditional insert in the store
questions.explanation: Only an atomic compare-and-set at the storage layer closes the race; a separate check then insert has a window between the two steps where both callers see the alias free.

questions.q: Deleting or expiring short links complicates one design choice above others. Which one?
options: 301 permanent redirects already cached by browsers and CDNs
Base62 encoding, since its alphabet cannot represent expiry timestamps
Key-value storage, which lacks any delete operation
Read replicas, which never receive tombstone records
questions.explanation: Once a browser caches a 301 it may never ask you again, so a deleted link keeps redirecting from client caches you cannot purge. Temporary redirects avoid that trap.

questions.q: A celebrity tweets one short link; traffic spikes 10,000x on that key. Which layer absorbs this best?
options: The primary database, scaled vertically for the event
A queue that buffers redirects until load subsides
Consistent hashing, which spreads a single key across many storage nodes
An in-memory cache layer (and CDN) serving that hot mapping
questions.explanation: One immutable key read repeatedly is perfectly cacheable, so replicated caches and CDN edges serve it from memory. Consistent hashing cannot split a single key.

questions.q: Rate limiting link creation matters most to prevent what?
options: Redirect latency spikes caused by bursts of clicks
Cache stampedes that occur when many codes expire simultaneously
Abuse: spam and phishing farms mass-generating disposable links
Exhaustion of the 62-character encoding alphabet
questions.explanation: Creation is the abuse surface: bulk-generated links cloak malicious destinations and can get your domain blacklisted. Keyspace exhaustion is not a realistic worry at 62^7.

questions.q: Why do many shorteners pre-generate unused codes into a 'key pool'?
options: Pooling lets codes be encrypted in batches for safety
Creation just pops a ready key, avoiding hash retries or counter contention
Unused codes must age before browsers will accept them
It guarantees codes sort chronologically for analytics
questions.explanation: Uniqueness work moves offline to a background generator, so the online write path is a single fast pop with predictable latency and no coordination on the hot path.

questions.q: Estimate storage: 100M new links/year, about 500 bytes per mapping with metadata. Ignoring replication, five years is roughly:
options: 2.5 GB, easily fitting in one server's memory
25 GB, requiring a small dedicated disk array
250 GB, manageable on a single modern database node
250 TB, demanding a large distributed storage cluster
questions.explanation: 100M times 5 years is 500M rows, and 500M times 500 bytes is 250 GB. That fits one node, so sharding here is driven by throughput, not capacity.

questions.q: Sequential base62 codes let attackers enumerate links. Which mitigation keeps O(1) generation without a collision-check loop?
options: Apply a keyed permutation/bijection of the counter before encoding
Truncate a salted SHA-256 hash of the URL and retry whenever collisions occur
Randomize only the first character of each sequential code
Encrypt stored URLs so enumeration reveals nothing useful
questions.explanation: A format-preserving permutation such as Feistel or a multiply-by-odd-modulo-2^n scrambles counters into unpredictable codes while staying one-to-one, so uniqueness is still free.

questions.q: You must guarantee a redirect is never served for a link deleted for phishing, while keeping edge caches. Which design meets it?
options: Keeping long TTLs at the edge plus running a weekly purge of flagged codes
Short TTLs plus active invalidation/purge of flagged codes at the edge
Serving all flagged domains from a separate analytics cluster
Moving flagged mappings to a slower storage tier immediately
questions.explanation: Explicit purge removes the entry immediately, and a short TTL bounds exposure if a purge is missed. Long TTLs with weekly cleanup leave days of live phishing redirects.

questions.q: Multi-region active-active: a link created in Europe is clicked in Asia 100ms later and must resolve. Which approach handles this with lowest write latency?
options: Synchronous cross-region quorum writes on every single creation
A single global primary region handling all link creations
Creating links only in the region where clicks are expected
Async replication plus fallback read to the origin region on local miss
questions.explanation: Writes commit locally and replicate in the background, so creation stays fast; a rare local miss pays one cross-region read, which still returns the correct target.
